Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a bill of great importance and one which no one in the committee should vote for lightly, without consideration as to whether it needs modification. I propose at the outset to state my conclusions in the hope that I may thereby indicate a certain moderation, and perhaps get sympathetic consideration for the succeeding remarks I shall make.
I am not prepared to say that with the knowledge the government has there may not be a valid argument for the continuance of these powers, or some of them, for a period. But there are two points I wish to put before the committee the first of which has reference to the duration of the bill, which I hope very much the committee will agree to amend by putting a time limit on it. The second point I wish to bring to the attention of the committee is a matter which was put before the standing committee, and unsuccessfully, of trying to introduce at least some moderation, at least some beginning to a return to freedom which at the present time this bill entirely denies.
I wish to say a word about the importance of the bill. I put this particularly to supporters of the government; we should face the fact that we are trying slowly and painfully-and it is still doubtful whether successfully-to emerge from quasi-socialism with as large a measure of freedom as we can. Hon. gentlemen who sit to my immediate left will, I take it, favour this bill. But to them I should like to point out what was said the other day by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), something which I commend to all the members of his party. These were his words:
We are not opposed to private enterprise, but we demand that private enterprise shall take the risks if it takes the rewards.
I think that is a fair statement; I would not take away one wrord from it. But I suggest to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that he might clarify the ideas of some other members of his party, notably the genial member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine), and the sometimes genial member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), because they seem to me constantly to use words which are entirely repugnant to the view expressed in the words I have just quoted of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.
I believe it is worth saying this, because in my view the spirit in which we approach these things, particularly with the difficulties we are facing to-day, will be of great importance in the next few years. I resent more than I can say the remarks which I have heard in the house, remarks which were perhaps not made seriously, but which seem to indicate that any man who had been successful in private enterprise must have been either a hard, rapacious, overbearing man, or a crook. I am not saying this in respect of any particular person, nor do I suggest that those were the words used. But I do say that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has expressed a view in the matter which should be taken seriously by his supporters.
I suggest most earnestly that hon. members should consider carefully the powers given under this bill-rigid, uncontrolled, unlimited as they are. They should seriously consider whether it is necessary not only to give these powers, but to give them without any time limit. I had hoped, from the remarks of the Acting Minister of Finance when the bill was introduced, and when we passed second reading, that certainly he had an open mind on the subject of time. However, as I remember, he said later that the government had decided that it would leave the time unlimited.
As the acting minister has said, the government has decided, and I am never at all sure whether that means that the minister himself has. decided, or whether the government has made the decision. However that is a detail which perhaps is none of our business. At any rate, that was the attitude the acting minister took.
I ask the committee to look at these powers, and the reasons for which they were granted originally, and then I ask hon. members to consider whether it is necessary that these powers be continued indefinitely and in an unlimited fashion.
Foreign Exchange Control

The reason for asking these powers was, of course, the situation in which we found ourselves in 1939. Probably the basic reason was the expected flight of capital, particularly to the United States. After all, at that time Canada, a small country in point of population, was at war, whereas the United States, a large country was not at war. It would not have been surprising, therefore, if there had been a serious flight of capital, and I believe the use of these powers at that time was generally approved. I think the officials who exercised those powers exercised them with moderation, discrimination, sympathy and efficiency. I say that now so that nothing I may say later would seem to be a criticism of the way in which these powers were exercised.
I would say further that if ten years ago anyone had been asked to read this bill and to consider the powers it represents, he would have been horrified. He would have said, "Surely we have not come to that; surely we have not to give this board the power to search, the power to arrest, the power to make inquiries of all kinds, not by police officers, not by the ordinary officers of the crown but by agents of this board?" In war time we accepted that. I ask again, and I ask it as earnestly as I am capable of asking: Is it necessary to commit ourselves indefinitely to powers of that kind in a time which we call peace?
It is interesting to observe-this was frankly stated by the witness before the banking and commerce committee-that, as is natural, these powers were built up and based on inquiries and examinations made of the various foreign exchange control boards throughout the world. It is natural and to be expected that they would look at the German board among others. I am not criticizing that, but I suggest to members of this committee that it is worth recalling that it was powers just such as these which enabled Doctor Schacht to exercise the powers which he did. I suggest that when we consider these powers we should consider them as such. We should not consider them merely as powers which are exercised by amiable and pleasant gentlemen who have shown great discrimination and moderation in the use of them, but as powers which may not always be exercised1 by those same pleasant gentlemen, which may some time get into the hands of people we may not find so agreeable and so pleasant and who may find these powers most convenient for purposes of their own.
I want to make the point that there has been virtually no relaxation or diminution in

peace time of the powers which were contained in the wartime act. If there are any changes, they are trivial and of no consequence.
Briefly, let us look at the powers. I will divide them into two groups. There is the power over ordinary current account transactions, and there is the power over capital account transactions. The power over current account transactions, that is to say ordinary buying and selling between Canada and other countries, I think it is fair to say has been exercised in the least oppressive manner. Apart from the fact of getting permission and having to fill out forms, this power has been operated with as little inconvenience as possible. The board has the power to scrutinize and approve every transaction. What it exercises this power for is to make sure that transactions are genuine. An illustration given in the committee was that the board would not approve a transaction where some one wanted to buy a motor car in United States, and where obviously the price being paid was an inordinate one, one which would indicate that it was really concealing the export of capital. If you are going to have power at all, it is reasonable to expect that it would have to be exercised in that way.
The second power is over capital account transactions. In capital account transactions we have reached the point where the expert authorities whom we have set up have full control. I believe in experts as much as anyone, but I should like to quote a little jingle I heard the other day. Experts should be used for advice and not for control; experts should be on tap and not on top.
I want to come back to the experts, for whom as individuals I have great respect. The experts now exercise not only economic judgment but moral judgment or quasi-moral judgment on what the citizens of this country are doing. Let me give an illustration. If I am a manufacturer in Canada and wish to invest money in the United States to build a factory, other things being equal, the permission is likely to be granted. If the hon. member for Lake Centre wishes to make an investment in some stocks in the United States, it is almost certain that permission will be refused. I said to the experts, "Does not that mean that you are really exercising moral judgment?" I said to them, "I am more sympathetic to the idea that the man who wishes to invest money in the United States, if it is for the purpose, let us say, of building a factory there, should be permitted to do so, but I do not know whether a man who wishes to invest money there may not be doing just as useful an act." I could not possibly be sure, but this board is set up and it has power

Foreign Exchange Control
to scrutinize such acts and to reach a conclusion. Again I ask hon. gentlemen to consider whether they wish to give an indefinite life to a bill which does that.
One more argument, in fact almost the greatest argument given by the witness before the committee, was that it was necessary to establish this control in order to carry out our obligations under Bretton Woods. That is a complicated and difficult question, and I do not propose to go into the details at the moment. I have tried to consider it as well as I can. I believe that view is a very narrow, limited and basically unsound view. If I understand Bretton Woods correctly, it is set up for the purpose of preventing depreciation in exchanges. My feeling is that our duty is to maintain stability and to argue that the foreign exchange control board is necessary merely for the purpose of carrying out our obligations under Bretton Woods is to me in principle unsound and untenable.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext: I think he said that was only one of the reasons.

subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext:
With deference to the minister I want to say that I read the evidence the other day. I think it is correct to say that it was not stated to be the exclusive reason, but on reading the evidence I was surprised to find the extent to which it was based on that. My own feeling, for what it is worth is that a more basic reason is that probably our trade with the United States will be out of balance for the next months, and that at the present time until sterling is made convertible we are not able to settle our deficits in the United States with sterling balances.
In considering this question of financial control we are in danger of being lulled into a false sense of security. I think we are in great danger of not appreciating the importance of this bill. In the case of other departments I think we have clear evidence which will demonstrate that they hope that the controls will eventually be done away with. I think the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) has indicated that, although sometimes I feel that he is building up new controls almost as fast as the old ones are done away with; nevertheless many of the old ones have been done away with. I think the same can be said of other ministers. I think that is because those departments have had a larger admixture of ordinary business men who have returned to their old occupations, and probably that has hastened relaxation of controls.
I submit to the committee that there has been no sign whatever of any disposition on 63260-278
the part of the Department of Finance to relax controls. I further suggest, that if this bill stays on our statute books for five years it will just rivet tighter all these fetters which we accepted as necessary during the war. There is another reason, and I put -this forward with great earnestness and with great respect to the experts. What are the experts? Let us consider what they are. Let me say again that I think they are useful people. Those of us who are not experts, who must rely perhaps only upon common sense, are helped by the advice of experts but, I thiu* in the last analysis decisions have to be left to men of common sense, and we hope men of some experience. Happily the experts are always divided. You are never left entirely alone when you disagree with some of them.
Here we have a situation where these people have had almost unlimited power for seven years. I ask any man in this house if he thinks it would be easy after he had had unlimited power for seven years, power which he feels he has exercised well, when he is much more articulate in talking about matters of finance than other people, to give up any of those powers? He would not give up a tittle of them. I made the suggestion-I do not know whether there was any great merit in it-that there should be a kind of token of a beginning of the restoration of a little freedom. But I was told that it would spoil the pattern, it would spoil the picture; there would be a little blur somewhere. That is the only thing I could make out of it.
I have great respect for the experts, but I think there is great danger in this. Experts believe that they are alw'ays dealing with exact things. Some experts are. If you are an expert in nuclear physics you can pretty well predict what will happen, although at Bikini the experts were not entirely in agreement. Generally speaking, though, they can predict exactly what is going to happen. But I charge that we have experts in finance who believe that finance is an exact science and that you can predict exactly what is going to happen there. I suggest to members of the house who are practical common sense business men that that is perfect nonsense, because it leaves out our good old friend human nature. I suggest that not in any partisan way, because this is far too important a matter to put it on any partisan basis. I have the hope that we may still persuade the minister to put this on an annual basis so that we can have another look at it, and I shall suggest later the reasons which I hope may be convincing. If we cannot relax it this year, when are we going to relax it?

Foreign Exchange Control

Shall we repeal the act? Will the government want that? No. These are things that are being put out of the sight of parliament so that parliament will have no chance to consider them further. I am not enough of an expert on procedure to know how it could come up again next year.

speechtext:
That has not been a rewarding line of effort.
Now I want to say a word about the business community. I might be told that I am making a lot of fuss about nothing. The minister would not put it so crudely, but he might more delicately. He might fairly say: You are making a lot of fuss about this. But let us see what happened before the committee. Was the business community there to raise any questions? No; and I will tell you why they were not there-and this is perhaps the most important thing of all the important things that I have to say this morning. I will tell you 'why they were not there. First of all because business people do not like to come down here and say things that are unacceptable to the powers that be. The officials in the department have great power. I want to press that. I am not joking; I believe it with all my heart.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext: It is an interesting observation, anyway.

subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext:
I believe it is a true observation, which is much more important. Let us look at the facts. Our national income has doubled over ten years. Why? Because the dominion government was in business, because more than half our business was government business. Is there any mystery, then, in saying that people are a little shy of coming down here and saying things that governments do not like? Just examine the extent to which government is in business of all kinds, and see how much the income of business, even of the banks, depends on the good will of the government and of the governor of the Bank of Canada and the financial authorities. That is as true as we are standing here. That is the first thing.
The second thing-and I want to be frank about this and say that this is not so creditable to the business community-is that along with others it has been lulled into a false sense of
IMr. Macdonnell.]
security. They have a helpless feeling, if you like, and perhaps there may be some excuse for it. At any rate they were not here partly because they were afraid, and partly because -I say this in the hope that they may hear it-they have not considered this seriously enough. The third reason-and this is perhaps still less creditable to the business community, but I will say it because I am trying to be a witness to what I believe to be the truth-is that there are some people in the business community who have rather liked controls. I should like to quote to them what I quoted this morning from the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar. Free enterprise, do not let us forget, in spite of all that has been said against it, has done remarkable things. Those who believe in it have to accept what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said. He said that if they are going to have the rewards, they must take the risks. I would reverse it and say that if they take the risks they must have some rewards. But at the present time a great many people are busy trying to arrange matters so that free enterprise cannot function, so that controls will damp it down.
Just let me repeat that. I want to say that if the business community were not here it was because they were afraid of this government's powers, and that is what power does. Those who exercise it, however sincere they may be, come to believe that ordinaiy people cannot look after their own affairs. I said to one of these experts, "It is really impossible for you to believe that ordinary people like ourselves can look after our own affairs." I am serious about that. If I had had that power for seven years I might feel as they do. They would have to jump out of their intellectual skins before they can believe we can carry on without their controls. They believe that they have greater wisdom and that they must tell us what to do.
An able lawyer made a remark to me that I think very interesting. He was a great cross-examiner and dialectician. The purpose of the bill, we are informed, is to stabilize exchange and have our foreign exchange resources used to the best advantage. It will undoubtedly take some time for the business of the world to return to normal conditions after the upheaval of war, and a stabilized exchange would, I believe, assist in restoring the flow of goods and services between Canada and other countries.
I am not a financial expert, nor have I had any experience in international trade; consequently I am not in a position to make constructive suggestions which would further the purpose the government has in mind. But what strikes me about the bill is this, that it was promoted, planned and drafted by men [DOT]whose minds were so centred on currency and exchange that they overlooked the rights and liberties of the citizens of this country.
This bill, if it becomes law-and it will become law7 in its present form unless members on the government side take exception to some of its provisions-sets up a board of civil servants to buy and sell exchange at rates they will fix, to supervise and regulate the business transactions of our exporters and importers-	.

-to supervise the business transactions of our exporters and importers, and to control the assets and in consequence the movements of everyday people of this country. It is by this means that the government proposes to control the rate of exchange.
The bill is not limited in time to the transitory period from war to peace. It sets up a controlled economy in currency, securities and the export and import of goods for an indefinite period.
I favour a stabilized exchange during the transitory period from war to peace, if it can be brought about without interfering with the rights and liberties of the everyday people of this country: I believe it should be possible to enact legislation which would achieve that end. But if it is impossible, and that end can be achieved only by depriving the people of this country of the control of their property, and as a result, of their movements, as this bill does, then I am opposed to a stabilized exchange.
I hold the view that the people of Canada should have the right to do what they like with what belongs to them, provided that they do not interfere with the rights of other people. If this bill becomes law it will deprive them of many of the rights they possessed prior to the war.
Among other things the bill provides in section 25-and I am by no means giving a complete list-that no person in this country shall export any property from Canada without permission of the board.
In section 26 it provides that no person in Canada can import any property into Canada without permission of the board, but the board is not to withhold its permission to export or import when a fair value is being paid for the goods in a currency approved by the board.
By section 27 it provides that no person in Canada shall sell or assign his securities either inside or outside of Canada to any person who is not resident in Canada, unless he gets permission from the board.
It provides that no person in Canada can purchase any securities either outside or inside of Canada from a non-resident unless he gets permission from the board.
It provides in section 29 that any Canadian who owns securities outside of Canada must bring them into Canada when ordered by the board.
It provides in section 31 that no person residing in Canada can set up a trust fund, except by will, without obtaining permission from the board.
It provides by section 31 that no person in Canada shall assign or deliver to a non-resident any property situated in Canada or elsewhere, and no person residing in Canada can give any property to a non-resident without a permit from the board.
It provides by section 32 that no person in Canada may render any service to a person residing outside of Canada without authority, but must charge him and obtain payment within six months unless he obtains a permit from the board.
It provides by section 49 that the board can prohibit any person from exercising any control over his own property whenever it sees fit.
It provides by section 51 that the board can compel a person to transfer his property to a trust company, the costs of that company being a first charge on the property.
Let me give a few examples of the power the 'board will have under this bill if it becomes law in its present form. If you or I have a relative or friend in dire need living outside of Canada, in Ireland, Great Britain, the United States or some other country, whom we want to help and whom before the war we could have helped without asking permission of any one, under this bill we cannot help that person unless we get a permit from the board.
If you or I want to go on a trip to the United States or any other country, before leaving Canada we must present ourselves before a customs officer and answer all the questions that may be put by him relating to the property we are taking with us. If the customs officer does not believe us and thinks we have other property concealed on our person, he may search us and he may search our luggage. He has the power to arrest and seize and detain our property. Those provisions are contained in section 48.
If you or I want to leave Canada for an indefinite period and go to Australia, Scotland or any other country, either within or without the British commonwealth and empire, we cannot take with us what belongs to us unless we get a permit from the board. If we happen to be people of some means, that permit will probably be refused and we shall not be able to take with us what belongs to us.
If a farmer sells his farm with the intention of moving to the United States and going to work there, and the United States immigration authorities have given him permission to enter the country, the board will not pre-

Foreign Exchange Control

vent him from going but they will refuse in most cases to let him take with him what belongs to him if it amounts to over $5,000.
If, for what we consider good reasons, you or I have certain securities deposited outside of Canada the board can order us to bring them into Canada.
If you or I have a friend outside this country to whom we are under an obligation, we cannot render him a service or do any work for him without making him pay us for it within six months unless we obtain a permit from the board.
The long and the short of the matter is that this bill deprives the people of Canada of the right to control their own property and places that control in the hands of a board of civil servants.

Not at all.
When the war broke out the majority of the people in this country did not object to a curtailment of their freedom and liberty under the powers conferred' upon the government by the War Measures Act and later by the National Resources Mobilization Act. The people believed that the government should have extraordinary powers while Canad'a was fighting for its existence. The war is over now, and these dictatorial powers should end. But instead of being brought to an end they will be perpetuated if we pass this bill.
The board to be set up under this bill is to take the place of the foreign exchange control board, which was established by order in council early in the war. It is being given practically the same dictatorial powers that that board possessed. According to section 11 the board will consist of six high-ranking civil servants. We are told that these men would not think of exercising the great powers conferred on them unreasonably or harshly, but would use the best judgment and tact in the exercise of the extraordinary powers that are being conferred on them. The only way in which we can form an opinion of how they will conduct themselves is to recall how they have conducted themselves in the past. I propose now to give a few instances- perhaps the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario never heard of these-of how the present board and its two hundred or so satellites have carried on their duties.
This board has seized the money of many innocent people who live near the international boundary line. A Canadian Pacific employee, who lives at McAdam Junction, New Brunswick, and who does most of his work in the state of Maine, addressed a letter

containing about $20 to a relative living in Maine who had assisted him when there was illness in his family. This money had been earned in the United States by a man who worked in the United States, but the letter happened to be mailed from a Canadian post office to a person living in Maine. The money was seized and it has never been returned.
The president of a large United States corporation who was in Vancouver on business was unable to pick up a coat that belonged to him because of the hurry to catch a train for home. He asked a friend whom he knew would be in his town in the course of a few days to bring the coat with him. The friend got the coat and put it in his valise, but he removed a bill-fold which he noticed was in the pocket. He was asked by the Canadian customs officer about the money he was taking to the United States and he gave them the particulars. The customs official asked him what was in the bill-fold, and he said he had not looked at it, that he was taking it to a United States friend who had left it in Vancouver. It was opened and was found to contain, if I remember correctly, $S0 in United States funds. The customs official confiscated it, but when the owner heard of what had happened he telegraphed to the state department in Washington and the money was returned. But the railway conductor in McAdam Junction has not got his money back yet.
A young boy living in New Brunswick near the Maine border earned $90 by working in the potato fields. This was the first money this boy had ever earned. The evening he arrived home with it one of his friends suggested that they drive across the line to the state of Maine which was only a few miles away. When he got to the border the $90 was seized.
An old man living near the border who was in the habit of passing from New Brunswick to Maine had about $90 seized. A member of parliament who approached the Minister of Finance on his behalf was informed by the minister that the regulations were not intended to be used in this way and that he would take up the matter with Mr. Graham Towers, the chairman of the board. A few days later the Minister of Finance informed the member that he had seen Mr. Towers, who said that they had taken money from so many people-this is the effect of his Words I am not quoting them exactly-that if they paid it back to one they would have to pay it back to all and it might lead to complications. The

Foreign Exchange Control
minister added that he did not care to interfere with the work of the board. That is the way this bureaucratic board carries on. Money was taken in this way from many innocent people and in some cases it has not been returned to them.
There was a case in New Brunswick to which I would direct the attention of the committee. One morning a woman set out for the bank with $300 for the purpose of paying a note which was due that day. When she got to town she found that the bank had not opened, so she proceeded to visit her daughter. Her daughter suggested that they drive across to a town in the United States which was only a few miles away. When they got to the border the $300 was seized by the Canadian officials. Later that day the woman reported the seizure to the manager of the Royal Bank of Canada where the note was due, and the manager said he would write to Ottawa. The woman never got her $300 back, but it was sent by the board to the branch of the Royal Bank of Canada to pay off the note. The fact that the chairman of the board was at one time in the employ of the Royal Bank of Canada is a mere coincidence.

His brother, who was to accompany him, went to the bank for the purpose of obtaining United States funds. In due time the manager of the bank received a most discourteous letter from the board censuring him for advancing the money without obtaining permission. The fact that time might have been a matter of life and death did not enter into their calculations.

If bureaucratic government is to continue, if we

want to set up a new form of despotism, all we have to do is to pass this bill in its present form.
Under our constitution property and civil rights are a matter for the provinces, and I doubt very much that parliament has the power to pass an act of this kind, despite the opinion-and it was a vague opinion, if I may say so, not backed up by authority-of the justice department.
I want to point out that when a Canadian citizen goes to the board, hat in hand, for a permit to do this or to do that, the board in granting or refusing the permit is not governed in most instances by any law that parliament has passed, but acts as it sees fit.
The members of this house were elected by the people in their constituencies to make the laws, and we are responsible to the people who elected us for what we do here when'the next election comes round. But if we pass this bill and give powers to the board to make the laws under which it grants or refuses permission, if we place in the hands of the board powers that were given us under our democratic form of government-

I would refer for a moment to the report made a year or two ago by the committee on civil liberties of the Canadian Bar Association. The report says:
Laws should be enacted by parliament directly. The essence of democracy is that people govern themselves through their fully chosen representatives . . . The delegation of legislative power is not in the spirit of democratic institutions, the purpose of which is that the people's elected representatives alone shall make the laws . . .
Governments that try to place in the minds of the people the same respect for orders and regulations of delegated bodies as for public laws of parliament simply degrade the whole system to the level of dictatorship.
Parliaments, in introducing into democratic institutions the methods of dictatorship, render democracy odious to the people, who, in consequence, will be thrown into all sort of novel theories and political systems, hoping thereby to escape despotism, which they abhor.

Let me give my reason for saying this. A judge on an ex parte application can authorize a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and another person to enter and search if necessary by force any building for property which he has reasonable grounds for believing is liable to forfeiture, and seize property and carry it away if he finds it, and detain it from the lawful owner for ninety days, while the board makes up its mind if it will prosecute the owner. If a search is made and no property is found, if the officer, inspector or person had reason to suspect that property liable to seizure would be found, he shall not be liable to any prosecution or action on account of any search or detention of property, although he may have used force, as he is given the right to do, and in consequence done damage, committed assault, or committed trespass.

That does not make it any better. That is a pretty poor answer, it seems to me. Laws of this kind, I have no hesitation in saying and I do say, put the subject at the mercy of the police and pave the way for wrongdoing and abuse of power by civil servants.
Now let us see how the bill proposes to treat the people who are arrested by the board or its officials, with or without warrant, or are charged with violating any of its provisions or the regulations that are made by the board when they are dealing with their own property.
The bill says that no prosecution shall be commenced without the consent of the attorney general, and if this were so it might ameliorate to some extent the harshness of the legislation, although the right to lay a charge should not be subject to the permission of the executive. But the bill does not so provide; for it goes on to state that a person can be arrested and put in gaol notwithstanding the consent of the attorney general is not obtained, and then it goes on to say that no further proceedings shall be taken.
Well, you go pretty far when you put a man in gaol, and it does not help him much to provide, after you get him there, that no further proceedings shall be taken without the consent of the attorney general. I regard those provisions as most objectionable. A man can be arrested and locked up, and I presume he will remain in gaol unless bail is provided, until the board sees fit to notify the attorney general, and until the attorney general, who may be on his holidays, sees fit to consider the matter. If he decides that the man should not be prosecuted, that there were not good and sufficient grounds for his arrest, the accused apparently has no relief for the wrong he has suffered and the bill does not provide how he is to get out of gaol. If on the other hand the attorney general decides that the prosecution should continue, not that it should be commenced, as the bill states, the bill provides that the judge is to presume that the accused did not have permission from the board to act as he did or had not been exempted by the board from doing as he did. The burden of proof is put on the accused to prove his innocence.
Now, sir, it is a fundamental principle of British justice that a person is presumed innocent until he is proven guilty, and that the crown must prove the guilt of the accused, and that the accused must have the benefit of every reasonable doubt. These principles have been justified by long experience throughout the years.

I shall endeavour to pay heed to your suggestion, Mr. Chairman, that the principle of this bill was adopted by this house some time ago. May I say, however, that in regard to many of these technical measures it is impossible to know the ramifications and the full import of a resolution until one sees the bill itself. I recall that on more than one occasion, if not in this precise instance, a discussion of the principle itself was permitted after the standing committee had reported back to the house. Certainly in a bill such as the one we are now considering there are very many technical matters which could not be known in advance. So if in a sense what I say is a report on the findings of the committee, I hope you will pardon me.
In the committee we found that if we were to have foreign exchange control we must have all or nothing. Apparently there was no halfway measure. At the same time, however, we find that those who operate the foreign exchange control board have great discretion, and that the satisfactory or otherwise operation of this board depends a great deal if not entirely upon how those who are in authority -and I am speaking not of those in political 
authority but of those in administrative authority-exercise their discretion from time to time.
One or two matters were brought up this morning by various speakers, to which I should like to refer. First the hon. member for Acadia wondered how it was that the progressive Conservative party could support the Bretton Woods agreement and at the same time dislike the present bill to set up a permanent foreign exchange control board. May I say to the hon. member that many of us in this party hope that Bretton Woods and the international monetary fund which will be established under that agreement will prevent some of the disruptions of foreign exchange, and thereby of foreign trade, which took place in pre-war years, and which were among the indirect causes of war itself. We hope the nations subscribing to the Bretton Woods agreement will include most of the trading nations of the wprld, and we hope those nations will not again engage in currency warfare. A nation which wanted to increase its exports reduced its currency in terms of the currency of other nations, and in this way the goods of the exporting country were made cheaper. In return they got money, usually hard money from the United States or some other country where they wanted to buy in future. But this process of lowering the value of exchange led to competition and to great difficulties, and it is something we hope Bretton Woods will obviate in the future.

subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext: Does the hon. member see any sign of trade wars lessening soon as a result of the Bretton Woods agreement?

subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext:
I am hopeful, as I think most of the world is, that the signatories to Bretton Woods will include most if not all the trading nations, and that those signatories will live up to the agreement which they undertook when they signed the Bretton Woods pact. If they do, there will be strict limitations on the extent of any change they may make in the value of their currency. They may not alter their currency by more than ten per cent without the approval of the governing body; up to ten per cent it may be done without approval, though they must first consult the international board. It is hoped that by this means currency wars will be avoided in future.
The hon. member for Acadia also said that if we did not have an exchange control board, exchange rates would be at the mercy of and subject to all the hazards of speculators. May I say to the hon. member that in the normal working of exchange rates the exchange values of different currencies wers the reflection of

Foreign Exchange Control
economic events in different countries. They were the result of the work, labour and trading of the ordinary man who did business with other countries. They were not the result of speculators or others who would say, " We want the rate to be so and so, so that we can make a profit." They came about substantially by the working of natural economic forces. What the present arrangement of having a control board does is to make of every Canadian a speculator, willy-nilly. The ordinary individual has no choice in the matter at all. As a citizen and taxpayer he is subject to the risks of exchange through the foreign exchange control board. And if one does not fully realize what the situation is, when we placed the Canadian dollar on a parity with the United States dollar the loss, while not yet revealed to us, is estimated-a very good guide being given to us by those who are in control -at approximately S150 million. So that, spread over 11 million or 12 million people it is easy to see that in a sense we are all made speculators and made to bear a loss which we would not otherwise have to bear.
Again, the hon. member said that Bretton Woods implies exchange control. Even the Minister of Finance when he introduced the resolution on which this bill is based said there were three policies which would be followed, and one of them was exchange stabilization, or an exchange equalization fund. I believe that would work with greater satisfaction to Canada and to our people than would the present hidebound, iron-clad system of exchange control over even the most petty transactions with the United States or with other countries.
While as a result of the exigencies of the war most other countries do have foreign exchange control to-day, we have in the United States the great example of a strong economic power, similar in many respects to our own, only larger, and to some extent more self-sufficient. That country does not have exchange control, nor, so far as one can see, is there any likelihood of its having it. I should also think that as soon as possible the United Kingdom will do away with exchange control, because so long as she has these controls, particularly on capital account, she can never again become the financial centre of the world. That position, occupied with such ability by Great Britain for so many years, brought to her a source of income which she cannot 'well do without, and gave her a position in world trade which was the envy of every other country.
May I point out that already Canada has become the third or fourth largest trading nation in the world, and the amount of foreign exchange bills resulting from that trading is
substantial. But these bills are now all cleared through New York, and a commission is paid to those engaged in financial business in that centre. If we were able to do without control in this country there is the possibility that just as other centres in Europe such as Paris, Brussels and Berlin did at a time when London was the paramount financial centre, so we might on this continent become a financial centre of some importance, and thereby add to our national income. But that cannot be attained so long as we have the rigid controls provided by this bill.
This morning the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) said that exchange controls will always be with us. Let us hope that we can get away from controls. Later I shall cite what the Minister of Finance said when he introduced the resolution. The hon. member for Cariboo implied that exchange rates had in the past been made by certain wealthy individuals in other countries. But may I tell him, as I have suggested to the hon. member for Acadia, that exchange rates were always made by the work and trade of all the people in a country. It is the result of all the transactions connected with the buying and selling of goods between our country and other countries that determines the exchange rates existing between those countries. That again is influenced by the cost of producing goods in one country as against producing them in another.
Exchange controls perpetuate or endeavour to perpetuate artificiality. We had an example of that on July 5 when suddenly, and without any warning to our people, the Canadian dollar became worth ten per cent more in terms of United States and sterling currency. That situation would not have come about with such abruptness if the ordinary working of the economic forces which are continuously at play were not under the poultice and the cover of the foreign exchange control board, and we should not have had the dire results in some of our industries which followed as a consequence of that ten per cent change overnight in our exchange rate.
Let me say a word or two about what I believe is the really important matter behind this bill. The dominion government has taken unto itself the management of our whole economy. The federal power ramifies through the life of every business man and every worker in the community, not only by way of taxation, but through price and wage controls. The dominion government in its offers to the provinces has undertaken to look after all unemployment in the event of bad times, and it will guarantee a fairly stable economy pro-

videdi that it is allowed to run the whole show. It will give to the provinces a bag of gold so that they can run their own shows in their own back yards. But if the dominion is to assume the responsibility for a managed economy, then there must be no one else's hand on the steering wheel. They must run all business. They must run the whole economy, to the point where it means that any other political power or any other political subdivision in Canada must become a nonentity.
We have seen what happened after five years, during which time the provinces leased their taxing powers in certain fields to the dominion.

Let me quote what he said, and I refer hon. members to page 2547 of Hansard:
We hope that it

Referring to the immediate future.

will be one which does not call for restrictive controls and we shall do everything in our power to bring this about.
I refer to those remarks in view of the absence of any time limit to this bill, and the refusal of the Acting Minister of Finance to adopt our suggestion that a time limit of a year, or even a slightly longer period, be put on this bill. Let me refer to what the Minister of Finance said on June 17, as reported on page 2548 of Hansard:
When the world returns to a more normal basis we shall have a fresh look at the question.
Surely in view of those two statements one might have expected to find a time limit here. But we did not. We hope that hon. members of this house who value freedom, who believe that this matter is one which may be useful to tide over an emergency, let us say until Bretton Woods comes into effect, will consider this matter. I made my statement when the resolution was introduced in this house. I was not against the exchange controls until the time arrived when we could have a look at them to find out what other nations are going to come in under the agreements. Surely within a year or two years this bill should automatically come before parliament again to see whether or not parliament thinks the restrictions on the normal activities of our people should be continued. I cannot see any reason why the government should not be agreeable to that suggestion.
Let us consider the position of our country in regard to foreign exchange in 1939, and whether it would have been better if controls had existed during the thirties. I asked in the committee how much better off Canada would have been in 1939, when of necessity we thought it was the correct thing to impose controls in order to strengthen our sinews of war, if we had had these controls foisted upon us during the period of the thirties. There was no satisfactory answer to that. We got through the war period, we handled our exchange, we had our controls when necessary and we were all agreeable to that. If we are going to adopt the control philosophy which is sponsored by this government we might as well have had those controls all during the twenties and the thirties. But to what purpose? They would have served no useful purpose.

What have we to fear in the future that we need these controls now? Reference is made to an exposed economy, but of course we as a trading nation are always exposed to other nations. If we buy too much, then we run short of United States dollars; if we sell too much and do not buy enough, then we have a surplus and some other country is embarrassed. Each country
Foreign Exchange Control

must look after its own economy; it must look after these matters, and not by exchange controls.
Are we likely to become an aggressor nation so that we shall need controls? The United States has not always been a friendly economic neighbour, but of necessity she has always been a friendly political neighbour. Controls during the last war did not save us. We ran short of United States exchange. But we had the Hyde Parle agreement. There is not much doubt that if we are in a crisis at some time in the future the United States will also be behind us or we behind them because we have the same philosophy of life. Neither country is an aggressor nation, and just as they came to our financial aid in 1942 they will come to our aid again. In the meantime we could get rid of these controls and we could then trade freely, not only on current account but on capital account, with our cousins ih'the United States.
It was not pointed out in the committee by the witness for the government to what extent our external currency position is more hazardous now than it was in 1939. The Minister of Finance at page 2543 of Hansard reported that Canada's holdings of gold expressed in United States dollars amounted as of September 15, 1939, to 8393,000,000 and on December 31, 1945, they amounted to $1,508,000,000-holdings of gold and United States dollars at the end of the war about four times as large as we had at the beginning. I also remember, sir, the day when all that gold, securities and currency was transferred by truck to the vaults of the Bank of Canada, not to be under the control of the Bank of Canada, mark you, but to be under the control of the foreign exchange control board.
I wonder why some members are silent about this matter, because the foreign exchange control board holds all the gold, all the securities and all the treasury notes which form the national wealth of the country, and which are the guarantee of the bank notes issued by the Bank of Canada. Long before the hon. member for Kamloops was elected, I warned the House of Commons in committee of the whole, in committee of supply and in other committees that it was absurd to have Canada bank notes issued by the Bank of Canada when the securities were in the hands of the foreign exchange control board.
Who thought of that? The promise to pay is made by the Bank of Canada, and the
guarantee is in the hands of the foreign exchange control board. That is on record in Hansard. There is discrimination; there is disparity; there is something that I cannot understand about it. All that should be either in the hands of the Bank of Canada which issues the bank notes or under the Minister of Finance. These notes should be issued in the name of the Dominion of Canada instead of being issued by the Bank of Canada.
I do not think it can be said that I am not in order when I remind the committee of these things because they should be known to all hon. members. Hon. members should be warned against the excessive powers that have been given to the foreign exchange control board. Our Social Credit friends complain about the monetary policies of this government, but this is one reform they should advocate, that all the treasure of this country, all the gold and securities, all the wealth that is in the hands of the foreign exchange control board should be placed in the hands of the Minister of Finance so that he may be responsible to parliament for all financial legislation passed by this house. That would be an easy thing to do.
That is what was done in the past. That is following the tradition of Fielding, a Liberal; it is following the tradition of White, a Conservative; it is following the tradition of Jim Robb, one of the last Liberals who was Minister of Finance. I want those hon. members to leave aside all their abstractions and get down to brass tacks. I want them to advocate reforms that are practical, reforms that can be brought about. Instead of getting into new fields that are unknown to all they should get back to the sound traditions of the past so that we could have parliamentary control to prevent waste and foolish expenditures. If all the expenditures that have been made by the foreign exchange control board had been submitted to the rigid control of the house the financial condition of this country at the present time would be different from what it is.
I am not saying this to discourage my hon. friends of the Social Credit group or of any other party in this house; I say this in order to encourage them to learn the history of Canada, to learn the lessons of the past, to remember those things which were good in the past so that we may come back to them and improve conditions instead of making them worse.

We aim to replace the present capitalist system.
Then, under the heading of planning:
The first step in this direction will be the setting up of a national planning commission consisting of a small body of economists, engineers and statisticians, assisted by an appropriate technical staff.
Which to an extent might be either the wartime prices and trade board or the foreign exchange control board.

The commission will be responsible to the cabinet and will work in cooperation with the managing boards of the socialized industries.

Control of finance is the first step to the control of the whole economy. I point out that this is a socialistic enactment, and because it is I am fearful of it, fearful of the principle which places in government the management and control of our economic system. The control of production, of wealth, is the control of human life itself. The relationship between what we sometimes call money or credit and production is so intimate that if we yield up the control of these essential elements to the government we are yielding to it control over our persons as well as over our property.

I believe that the money we have voted in the past has done much over a period of years to relieve many of the unfortunate situations that have arisen. When we talk of a war memorial, why should we spend a colossal sum, to which it appears to me there is no limit, on this one city? After all, the men who volunteered and went overseas in the Canadian army came from every province of the Dominion of Canada. Very few people in this dominion find their way here in a period of a year or many years. If we are to spend a colossal amount of money on a war memorial, spend it in beautifying the capital cities of our provinces from which these men went to serve overseas.
I have no objection to spending money for the beautification of Ottawa. I believe it is a good thing to do. But why centre a national war memorial in this city? We have a national war memorial here now, the Peace Tower, which is a great memorial that compares with the memorial in Edinburgh which many of us have seen. I believe that if we are to do something worth while and want the people of this country to see something for the money spent we should spend this money in the provincial capitals throughout the dominion.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support wholeheartedly the principle of this bill and to endorse the remarks made by previous speakers from British Columbia and others who have supported the bill.
In a matter like this, I think we should certainly avoid taking a parochial outlook. This is a national matter in the national interest and I think we should maintain the correct perspective. I am as anxious as any other hon. member to see increased old age pensions, better social security benefits and that everything possible be done for the working people as a whole, but I cannot see any logic or sound argument in criticizing what, after all, is a small expenditure when one compares it with our national expenditures as a whole.
I have always been interested in taking around this building people from my own province of British Columbia, particularly young people. A nation does not live by bread alone, and when you take young people and older people around these buildings you have evidence of the fact when you see how inspired they are by the buildings and surroundings and by the fact that they have had an opportunity of visiting their national capital. I think, this proposal further to beautify the federal district will be an inspiration not only to individuals but to other cities in Canada, to every town and every village and to every Canadian who has an opportunity to visit this district. I am quite sure that, as the years go by, the greatly increased facilities for travel will enable [DOT] great numbers of Canadians to visit the national capital and have an opportunity personally to see the scheme as it is developed.

Mr. Speaker, being a representative of the most beautiful part of the capital area, I think I should rise in support of this bill and, in doing so, I think I am reflecting the feelings of all hon. members when they seriously consider this bill. Credit should be given where credit is due. In addition to commending the work of the commission, I think great tribute should be paid to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). When he came to Ottawa from another part of Ontario he immediately took an interest in the development of the greater Ottawa area. If the Prime Minister should ever consider leaving active politics in the near future or at any time I hope he will consent to remain as adviser to or perhaps act as a director of the federal district commission.
At times the people of Ottawa do not like it to be said that Ottawa should be beautified, because they feel that this city has a natural beauty which cannot be improved by human hands. The people of Ottawa support this plan because they are citizens of this country. In paying tribute to this capital city, they are only doing what other parts of the dominion are doing. I wish we all had the same spirit in connection with this bill. A while ago the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Argue) spoke in a prejudiced manner. He approached this subject as though the delay of the beautification of this area would bring about more social measures or do more socially for other
parts of Canada. He said also that this bill had not been timed properly. I think the only thing wrong with the timing is that it is a little late.
We should go ahead as quickly as possible with the beautification plan for this capital area. We in Ottawa would like to have the Greber plan made public as soon as possible. At times blame is placed on municipal, provincial or federal authorities because no one knows just where to place it, but you cannot really blame any authority until you know what the plan is going to be. In conclusion, I can only say that it is always difficult for an Ottawa member to insist too much that he is attached to this plan, but as one who was born and raised here and whose soul is in this centre I trust that the members will not consider this question in any other way than as citizens of this country and will do all in their power to make the Ottawa area a beautiful capital and the soul of this country.

The timing of this bill is particularly appropriate. During the war years it was proper and necessary to lay aside energies which would be devoted to this subject and direct them into more appropriate lines. But in any event, as the result of some activities in which I may properly claim some considerable part along with others, a committee of the two houses of parliament was set up in 1944 to deal with the subject, not of the development of the national capital as such, but with the agreement between the corpora-

tion of the city of Ottawa and the dominion government. I should like publicly to acknowledge the good work done by the members of all parties on both sides of the house who sat on that committee. To-night some reference has been made to the representations from other parts of the dominion. As a representative of a part of the city of Ottawa, I may say that I am wholly in accord with the sentiments expressed, and indeed I took my part, along with others, in suggesting that representation should be given to all parts of the country in order that the matter would be approached in a proper way and not in any election way. But I would point out to the members who have dealt with this subject and apparently share the views I hold on the matter, that they are not wholly accurate in reading the section of the bill in the way in which they do. In appointing the commissioners, the government may appoint thirteen from different parts of the country. Only two of the appointments are to be specific appointments from specific areas. Then there is a provision that five of the others shall come from the maritimes or the western provinces, Ontario and Quebec as the case may be. I would point out that there is nothing to prevent the government from appointing one member from each province, if the proper person is available, interested in the subject and prepared to give the time and energy which are required.
There is one other point I should like to emphasize. In the early speeches to-night a great deal of reference was made to the city of Ottawa as such, and the development of the city of Ottawa. That is not the correct view of this legislation. If hon. members will examine the subject more closely they will find that it deals with the development of the whole district, the capital area, and indeed the greater part of the area is outside the city of Ottawa. I hope that the mistake will not be made of viewing it solely as a city measure, because that is not supported by the facts.

When the war ended, the devastated countries around Holland were unable to send anything out, whereas Holland was in the right position to export bulbs, samples of which reached Ottawa, Montreal and Toronto.

Leading into Ottawa, the highways should be modernized by the federal authorities, because you cannot expect some little municipality two or three miles on the outskirts of Ottawa to bear the burden of the cost of a modern highway.
The approaches to a city have a wonderful effect on visitors who come in cars. We are living in the days of modernized vehicular traffic and we must have modernized highways. I went up the Gatineau two Sundays ago. What the great drawback is about visiting the 16,000-acre farm under the federal district commission is the lack of roads. I did not suffer greatly going over some of the rough corduroy gravel roads, but I said to the superintendent of the federal commission, Mr. Hay, " I doubt very much whether our United States visitors would ever come back to see the beautiful lakes in the Gatineau area after travelling over these corduroy roads." Regarding Confederation square, I used to wonder as a boy about the sentence in the good old book which spoke of "the quick and the dead", but it was not until I tried to get around Confederation square that I realized that the "quick" is if you get across, and the "dead" if you don't, for you are no more, so that the scriptural reference to the quick and the dead1 is being fulfilled down on Confederation square.

ing with the other members to maintain and develop this capital city of ours. I believe that these gentlemen deserve gratitude for the work they have been doing, and I hope that when this new commission is set on foot it will be deemed fitting to keep them as members to continue the good work they have been doing.
I listened to the statement of the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross) to the effect that the city of Toronto was a very fine city, though it had not been built with federal government money. I recognize that. In 1867 no question had arisen of having a capital city or federal district commission. We came into Bytown, Ottawa, and development proceeded in cooperation with the municipality. In other cities administration of streets and civic services is carried on by the municipal governments, and we do not want to invade their domain or take away their civic autonomy; we want to cooperate with them to try to develop this city. If Ottawa had not been the capital city of Canada, for all we know to the contrary it might have been a large industrial centre, because of its water power and other natural resources in the immediately surrounding district. I believe that there is understanding between the municipal and federal authorities, and that, with the passing of this bill, as the years go by we shall see this city expand and develop and become one of the finest of capital cities.

Mr. Speaker, as a member of the committee in 1944 I should like to join in the debate which has taken place this evening. It seems strange that so far in the debate, of all who have taken part, the three members from British Columbia have been the greatest supporters of the bill and the beautifying of this federal capital. Surely every one of us can and should take pride in our capital city.
I know that those who visit Washington usually come back full of enthusiasm, and while I realize that Canada, with twelve million people, cannot compete with the great country to the south of us, nevertheless we can have a capital which, will be the envy of many other lands. As a matter of fact we have here in Ottawa a great chance to make a splendid capital, for it is better in location even than Washington.
I was suprised to hear the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Burton) coming out against the appropriation for the beautifying of the capital city. During the recess I took time to hunt up some facts, and I am just going to remind him that it seems strange that a province, which in six years got over $96

So far as the bill itself is concerned, I think it is a good thing to have a federal district, but we should go slow in this matter in the next two or three years and remember that we are spending the taxpayers' money.
